lesson.title: Brown v. Board of Education: Overturning Separate but Equal
lesson.summary: In a unanimous 1954 ruling, the Supreme Court declared racially segregated public schools unconstitutional, discarding the separate but equal doctrine that had justified legal segregation for nearly six decades, though the ruling's promise took years, and in some places decades, to be realized.
lesson.body:
Since 1896, the Supreme Court's decision in Plessy v. Ferguson had provided the legal foundation for segregation across the American South and in parts of the North: separating people by race in schools, transportation, and public facilities was constitutional, the Court had ruled, so long as the separate facilities were roughly equal. In practice, the facilities set aside for Black Americans were almost never equal. Black schools in particular were routinely underfunded compared to white schools, with fewer books, older buildings, and lower teacher pay, even though the Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, guaranteed every citizen equal protection of the laws.

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, had spent decades building the legal strategy to challenge this system, chipping away at segregation through a series of earlier court cases before making a direct assault on Plessy itself. The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, led by attorney Thurgood Marshall, who would later become the first Black justice on the Supreme Court, brought together several segregation cases from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, and Delaware into a single case named for one of the plaintiffs, a Topeka, Kansas family whose daughter Linda Brown had to travel far from her home, past a white school, to reach the segregated Black school she had been assigned to attend.

On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously, nine to zero, in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion, declaring that segregated public schools were inherently unequal and therefore violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, even where the physical facilities themselves might be comparable. The ruling directly overturned Plessy's separate but equal doctrine as it applied to public education. The decision also arrived during the height of the Cold War and the anti communist fervor of McCarthyism, a period when the United States was trying to present itself abroad as a model of freedom in contrast to the Soviet Union. American segregation was a frequent and effective target of Soviet propaganda, giving the federal government its own reasons to want the issue resolved, even as domestic critics sometimes tried to paint civil rights activism itself as communist influenced, a tactic that made organizing more difficult and more dangerous for NAACP members and other activists during this period.

Winning the case in court did not mean segregation ended in practice. A follow up ruling in 1955, sometimes called Brown II, ordered that school desegregation proceed with all deliberate speed, a deliberately flexible phrase that many Southern school districts used as an excuse to delay for years. In 1956, more than one hundred Southern members of Congress signed the Southern Manifesto opposing the ruling, and some states pursued a strategy of massive resistance, including Prince Edward County, Virginia, which closed its entire public school system from 1959 to 1964 rather than integrate. The most famous early test came in September 1957 at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, where Governor Orval Faubus used the state National Guard to block nine Black students, known as the Little Rock Nine, from entering the school. President Eisenhower responded by federalizing the Arkansas Guard and sending elite U.S. Army paratroopers to protect the students and enforce the court's order. Brown established the legal principle that would underpin the civil rights movement for the next decade, but it also showed that a Supreme Court ruling alone could not overcome deeply entrenched local resistance without sustained pressure and organizing, which is exactly what the movement built next.
